theory.intro: Large or continuous datasets are organised into **grouped frequency distribution tables** using intervals called **classes**.
facts: A **class interval** groups numerical values. Classes need not have equal widths, but must avoid overlaps and cover the intended range without gaps; inequalities make boundaries clear for continuous data.
The **class centre** ($cc$) is the midpoint: $cc = \dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2}$.
Grouping data reveals broad trends, but **information about individual data values is lost**.
The **relative frequency** is $\text{Relative frequency} = \dfrac{f}{n}$, where $f$ is class frequency and $n$ is total observations.
**Relative frequencies** written as decimal proportions sum to $1$; percentages sum to $100\%$. Rounded entries may not sum exactly to these totals.
The **cumulative frequency** is the running total of frequencies up to and including that class.

For the **equal-width frequency histograms** used here, columns touch, the horizontal axis shows classes or class centres, and the vertical axis shows frequency. Equal-width histogram conventions do not require every grouped table to have equal-width classes.
A **frequency polygon** joins column midpoints at class centres and anchors to the axis at empty classes on each end.
A **cumulative frequency histogram** has column heights equal to the cumulative frequency of each class.
An **ogive** is a cumulative frequency polygon connecting the top-right corner of each column from height $0$.
steps: Determine the class interval and calculate the class centre.
Tally the data to find the frequency of each class.
Calculate the relative frequency and cumulative frequency.
Draw the histogram and polygon or ogive.

workedExamples.question_text:
Choose an ungrouped or grouped frequency table for each dataset and explain your choice.
(a) $5,5,6,6,6,7,7,7,7$.
(b) Whole-number measurements: $12,47,31,58,24,39,16,53,28,42,19,35$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Use an ungrouped table. There are only three distinct values across a small range.
(b) Use a grouped table. There are many different numerical values across a wider range.

workedExamples.question_text:
A table for continuous lengths uses classes $2-11$, $12-21$, and $22-31$ cm.
(a) Explain why these classes leave gaps.
(b) Replace them with classes covering $2<x\le32$ cm, including each upper endpoint.
(c) Explain the problem with using $2\le x\le12$ and $12\le x\le22$ instead.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) A length such as $11.5$ cm belongs to no class.
(b) Use $2<x\le12$, $12<x\le22$, and $22<x\le32$. Each boundary belongs to exactly one class.
(c) The classes overlap at $12$ cm, which belongs to both classes.

(a) $\begin{aligned}cc&=\frac{30+39}{2}\\&=34.5\end{aligned}$
(b) $\begin{aligned}cc&=\frac{120+140}{2}\\&=130\end{aligned}$
The second class centre is $130$ cm.

workedExamples.question_text:
Whole-number test marks are $12,18,21,25,29,32,34,37,38,41,45,49$.
(a) Construct a grouped frequency table using $10-19$, $20-29$, $30-39$, and $40-49$.
(b) Find the total number of students, the most frequent class, and the number scoring $30$ or more.
(c) Can the grouped table alone tell you exactly how many scored less than $35$? Explain.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Count each mark in its class.

| Mark | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $10-19$ | $2$ |
| $20-29$ | $3$ |
| $30-39$ | $4$ |
| $40-49$ | $3$ |

(b) $n=2+3+4+3=12$.
The most frequent class is $30-39$.
The number scoring $30$ or more is $4+3=7$.
(c) No. The grouped table does not show how the four marks in $30-39$ are split between $30-34$ and $35-39$. Individual values are lost.

workedExamples.question_text:
Plant heights, in centimetres, are $4.8,10.0,10.2,15.6,20.0,20.4,24.7,30.0,30.5,38.2$.
(a) Construct a frequency table using $0<h\le10$, $10<h\le20$, $20<h\le30$, and $30<h\le40$.
(b) Find the fraction and decimal relative frequency of plants taller than $20$ cm.
(c) Find the percentage of plants $10$ cm or less tall.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) An upper endpoint belongs to the class ending at that value: $10.0$ belongs to the first class, $20.0$ to the second, and $30.0$ to the third.

| Height (cm) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<h\le10$ | $2$ |
| $10<h\le20$ | $3$ |
| $20<h\le30$ | $3$ |
| $30<h\le40$ | $2$ |

(b) $n=2+3+3+2=10$.
There are $3+2=5$ plants taller than $20$ cm.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Fraction}&=\frac{5}{10}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}\text{Relative frequency}&=\frac{5}{10}\\&=0.5\end{aligned}$
(c) $\begin{aligned}\text{Percentage}&=\frac{2}{10}\times100\%\\&=20\%\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text:
The grouped table records waiting times.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3$ |

(a) Complete the cumulative-frequency column.
(b) Find the frequency of $10<t\le15$ by subtracting cumulative frequencies.
(c) Find the relative frequency of each class as a decimal.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Add each frequency to the previous running total.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9$ | $15$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12$ | $27$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3$ | $30$ |

(b) The frequency is $27-15=12$.
(c) Divide each frequency by the total $30$.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Relative frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6/30=0.2$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9/30=0.3$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12/30=0.4$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3/30=0.1$ |

workedExamples.question_text:
For $90$ measurements, all values satisfy $0<x\le50$. The first class $0<x\le10$ has frequency $12$. There are $34$ measurements with $x\le20$, $25$ with $x>30$, and $7$ with $x>40$.
Complete the frequency and cumulative-frequency columns for five classes of width $10$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Subtract cumulative counts to find individual class frequencies. Subtract the count above $30$ from the total to find the count through $30$.
$\begin{aligned}f_1&=12\\f_2&=34-12=22\\\text{Count with }x\le30&=90-25=65\\f_3&=65-34=31\\f_4&=25-7=18\\f_5&=7\end{aligned}$

| Class | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0<x\le10$ | $12$ | $12$ |
| $10<x\le20$ | $22$ | $34$ |
| $20<x\le30$ | $31$ | $65$ |
| $30<x\le40$ | $18$ | $83$ |
| $40<x\le50$ | $7$ | $90$ |

foundation.question_text: Find the class centre of the class interval $20 - 29$.
Calculate the class centre of the continuous class interval $140 \le h < 160$.

The grouped frequency table shows the test scores of a class.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Score}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 10-19&4\\ 20-29&7\\ 30-39&11\\ 40-49&8\end{array}$
Find the total number of students in the class ($\Sigma f$).

A dataset is organised into a grouped frequency table with frequencies $5, 12, 18, 10, 5$.
Find the cumulative frequency of the third class.

In a survey of $50$ people, a class interval has a frequency of $13$.
Calculate its relative frequency as a decimal.

The times taken by $40$ runners are grouped below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Time (minutes)}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 0<t\le10&7\\ 10<t\le20&13\\ 20<t\le30&12\\ 30<t\le40&8\end{array}$
What fraction of the runners took $20$ minutes or less? Give your answer in simplest form.

A student groups continuous lengths into $10\le x\le20$, $20\le x\le30$, and $30\le x\le40$ cm.
Explain why these classes do not communicate information clearly.
foundation.solution_text: The classes overlap at $20$ cm and $30$ cm. Each of these lengths belongs to two classes, so its class is unclear.

foundation.question_text:
The table records whole-number weekly study hours.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Hours}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 10-19&5\\ 20-29&7\\ 30-39&9\\ 40-49&4\end{array}$
How many students studied for $30$ hours or more?

development.question_text:
The commute times (in minutes) of $60$ workers are grouped below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Class interval}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0-9&6\\ 10-19&15\\ 20-29&22\\ 30-39&11\\ 40-49&6\end{array}$
Find the class centres ($cc$), the relative frequencies ($f/n$) as decimals, and the cumulative frequencies for all five classes. Round nonterminating decimal relative frequencies to $3$ decimal places.

The masses (in kg) of $80$ parcels at a post office are recorded in the table.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Mass (kg)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0 < m \le 2&16\\ 2 < m \le 4&28\\ 4 < m \le 6&24\\ 6 < m \le 8&12\end{array}$
Calculate the relative frequency of parcels heavier than $4$ kg.

The daily electricity usage of a household is grouped below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Usage (kWh)}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 10<u\le14&4\\ 14<u\le18&6\\ 18<u\le22&10\\ 22<u\le26&7\\ 26<u\le30&4\end{array}$
What percentage of days had usage greater than $18$ kWh? Round to the nearest whole percent.

Customer waiting times are grouped below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Waiting time (minutes)}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 0<t\le5&9\\ 5<t\le10&14\\ 10<t\le15&25\\ 15<t\le20&17\\ 20<t\le25&11\end{array}$
Complete the cumulative-frequency column for all five classes.
development.solution_text:
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Waiting time (minutes)}&\text{Cumulative frequency}\\ \hline 0<t\le5&9\\ 5<t\le10&23\\ 10<t\le15&48\\ 15<t\le20&65\\ 20<t\le25&76\end{array}$
The running totals are $9$, $9+14=23$, $23+25=48$, $48+17=65$, and $65+11=76$.

development.question_text:
A table for continuous lengths uses the classes $5-14$, $15-24$, $25-34$, and $35-44$ cm.
Replace them with classes covering $5<x\le45$ cm without gaps or overlaps. Use inequalities with each upper endpoint included.
development.solution_text:
The original classes leave gaps; for example, $14.5$ cm has no class.
Use $5<x\le15$, $15<x\le25$, $25<x\le35$, and $35<x\le45$.

development.question_text:
A grouped frequency table records the race completion times of $120$ runners in classes $20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59$ minutes. Completion times were recorded in whole minutes. The $20-29$ class has a frequency of $30$ runners.
Explain why it is impossible to determine the exact number of runners who finished in under $25$ minutes.
development.solution_text:
The table groups all times between $20$ and $29$ minutes into a single frequency count of $30$ runners.
Individual data values are lost during grouping, so we do not know how many of these $30$ runners finished in $20-24$ minutes and how many finished in $25-29$ minutes.

development.question_text:
The table records whole-number driving test marks.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Mark}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 50-59&5\\ 60-69&11\\ 70-79&19\\ 80-89&17\\ 90-99&9\end{array}$
Find the total number of candidates and the fraction scoring $70$ marks or more. Give the fraction in simplest form.

The cumulative counts of plant heights are shown below. All plants have $0<h\le50$ cm.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Height condition}&\text{Cumulative count}\\ \hline h\le10&8\\ h\le20&23\\ h\le30&55\\ h\le40&86\\ h\le50&102\end{array}$
Find the frequency of the class $20<h\le30$ cm.

mastery.question_text:
Rainfall readings, in millimetres, are:
$0.5, 10.0, 10.1, 19.8, 20.0, 20.1, 29.7, 30.0, 30.2, 39.4, 5.6, 15.3, 25.8, 35.1, 8.9, 18.2$.
Complete a grouped frequency table using $0<r\le10$, $10<r\le20$, $20<r\le30$, and $30<r\le40$. What percentage of readings are $10$ mm or less?

For $108$ measurements with $0<x\le50$, the first class $0<x\le10$ has frequency $15$. There are $39$ measurements with $x\le20$, $31$ with $x>30$, and $12$ with $x>40$.
Complete the frequency and cumulative-frequency columns for $0<x\le10$, $10<x\le20$, $20<x\le30$, $30<x\le40$, and $40<x\le50$.

Plant heights, in centimetres, are:
$10.0, 10.1, 19.9, 20.0, 20.1, 29.9, 30.0, 30.1, 39.9, 40.0, 40.1, 49.9, 5.2, 15.4, 25.6, 35.8, 45.3, 8.7, 18.6, 28.5$.
Complete a grouped frequency table using $0<h\le10$, $10<h\le20$, $20<h\le30$, $30<h\le40$, and $40<h\le50$. Which class has the highest frequency?
mastery.solution_text:
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Height (cm)}&\text{Frequency}\\ \hline 0<h\le10&3\\ 10<h\le20&5\\ 20<h\le30&5\\ 30<h\le40&4\\ 40<h\le50&3\end{array}$
$\Sigma f=3+5+5+4+3=20$
The classes $10<h\le20$ and $20<h\le30$ share the highest frequency of $5$.
